To verify that the depth signal resides in the features rather than the classifier,
we repeat the 6-generator LOGO evaluation using Logistic Regression and Random Forest
in place of XGBoost (Table~\ref{tab:alt-classifier}).
All other settings (the same 7 features, 3-class labels, and class-balanced downsampling) are
kept identical. For Logistic Regression we apply standard scaling to the features.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 across three classifiers. Each column shows the held-out generator F1. (6-generator LOGO; 3-class.)}
\label{tab:alt-classifier}
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lc cccccc}
\toprule
Classifier & Avg F1 & OLMo-2 & Py-1B & Py-2.8B & Qw-0.6B & Qw-1.7B & Qw-8B \\
\midrule
XGBoost          & 0.789 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.824 & 0.806 & 0.683 \\
Random Forest    & 0.790 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.825 & 0.807 & 0.684 \\
Logistic Regr.   & 0.725 & 0.719 & 0.781 & 0.740 & 0.745 & 0.743 & 0.624 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Both tree-based classifiers achieve LOGO F1 $\approx 0.79$,
and even a linear model reaches $0.725$, well above the $0.33$ chance baseline for
three classes.
The per-generator ranking is also consistent across classifiers
(Pythia-1B easiest, Qwen3-8B hardest),
confirming that discriminative power originates in the entropy and lexical features,
not in classifier capacity.
Ordinal-specific methods (CORAL \cite{coral_ordinal}, Frank-Hall \cite{frank_hall_ordinal}) achieve comparable F1 with overlapping CIs, which confirms that 3-class granularity provides insufficient resolution for ranking-aware losses to improve over standard multiclass classification.

\subsection*{Sampling Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{app:sampling-sensitivity}

To assess robustness to decoding hyperparameters, we regenerate Qwen3-1.7B continuation chains under three sampling configurations (the remaining five generators retain their default-configuration data) and re-evaluate the 6-generator LOGO pipeline (Table~\ref{tab:sampling-ablation}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Depth classification under varying sampling parameters. All other settings match the default pipeline. (6-generator LOGO; 3-class and binary.)}
\label{tab:sampling-ablation}
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lcc ccc}
\toprule
Config & Temp.\ & Top-$p$ & 3-class F1 & Binary F1 & $\rho$(entropy\_mean) \\
\midrule
Low        & 0.5 & 0.80 & 0.785 & 0.797 & $-0.694$ \\
Default    & 0.7 & 0.90 & 0.788 & 0.799 & $-0.602$ \\
High       & 1.0 & 0.95 & 0.726 & 0.733 & $-0.002$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The depth signal is robust to moderate sampling variation: low and default configurations differ by at most 0.3\,pp in both 3-class and binary F1, and entropy--depth Spearman correlations remain strongly negative ($\rho \leq -0.60$).
At high temperature ($t{=}1.0$, top-$p{=}0.95$), classification degrades by approximately 6\,pp and the entropy--depth correlation collapses to near zero ($\rho = -0.002$).
This is consistent with the hypothesis that depth features are shaped by the sampling mechanism (\S\ref{sec:discussion}): elevated temperature injects sufficient randomness to flatten the distributional drift that accumulates across generation steps, effectively masking the depth signal.
The practical implication is that depth fingerprinting applies reliably under standard decoding regimes but should not be expected to generalize to high-entropy sampling settings.

\subsection*{Per-Generator Performance}

Figure~\ref{fig:per-gen} visualizes per-generator LOGO performance.
Pythia models (1B, 2.8B) achieve highest F1, while larger models (Mistral-7B, Qwen3-8B) show degradation.
The scale effect (larger models $\rightarrow$ lower F1) is consistent with higher-capacity models generating text statistically closer to human writing.

\label{fig:per-gen}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate whether depth signal generalizes beyond Wikipedia by constructing generation chains from three additional domains: News articles, Academic abstracts, and Code documentation.
For each domain, we sample 200 seed texts and generate chains of depth 3 using three generators (Pythia-1B, Qwen3-1.7B, Mistral-7B).
The same 7-feature ensemble and LOGO protocol are applied.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-domain depth classification under LOGO evaluation (binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+). Three generators $\times$ 200 seeds per domain. Bootstrap 95\% CIs ($n$\,=\,1000).}
\label{tab:domain}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Domain} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{3-class F1} \\
\midrule
Code           & 0.754 & [0.737, 0.770] & 0.634 \\
News           & 0.746 & [0.726, 0.764] & 0.652 \\
Academic       & 0.739 & [0.720, 0.757] & 0.622 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All three non-Wikipedia domains achieve binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, which demonstrates that depth signal is not an artifact of Wikipedia text properties.

\paragraph{Domain $\times$ temperature interaction.}
Cross-domain generation used $t{=}1.0$, top-$p{=}1.0$ (vs.\ the main experiment's $t{=}0.7$, top-$p{=}0.9$).
Supplementary evaluation at $t{=}0.7$ reveals a domain $\times$ temperature interaction: the main Wikipedia experiment favors lower temperature ($t{=}0.7$ yields +6\,pp over $t{=}1.0$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), while cross-domain evaluation favors higher temperature ($t{=}1.0$ yields +3 to +11\,pp over $t{=}0.7$; News 0.746 vs.\ 0.712, Academic 0.739 vs.\ 0.628, Code 0.754 vs.\ 0.687).
This asymmetry likely reflects reference-model calibration: Pythia-410M, trained predominantly on web text, detects subtle per-step drift in Wikipedia but requires larger distributional divergence (produced by higher temperature) to detect depth signal in out-of-distribution domains.
This finding suggests that reference model selection is a key factor for cross-domain deployment of depth fingerprinting.

\paragraph{3-class inversion as DDR evidence.}
In the cross-domain setting, 3-class F1 (0.62--0.65) falls below binary F1 (0.74--0.75), reversing the pattern observed in the main experiment (3-class 0.762 $>$ binary 0.694).
This inversion reflects degraded gen-0 vs.\ gen-1 separation: the Pythia-410M reference model is calibrated to Wikipedia text, so its baseline entropy estimates are less discriminative for out-of-domain human text and compresses the feature distance between gen-0 and gen-1.
The binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) is unaffected because both classes are generated under identical domain and decoding conditions; recursive drift is a relative change that does not depend on absolute calibration.
This pattern provides additional evidence that DDR captures generation-process invariants rather than domain-specific text properties: depth signal remains robust even when the human-vs-machine boundary becomes less distinct.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects and enable controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base); these comparisons use earlier LOGO subsets (5--6 generators) predating the full 8-generator expansion in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}.
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730), rewriting (0.737), and paraphrastic chains (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), which suggests that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
The reference model dependency (Pythia-410M, English-centric pretraining) limits non-English applicability and adds inference overhead relative to surface-feature-only approaches.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A temperature ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows that performance improves at lower temperature ($t{=}0.5$: $+$10.4\,pp) but degrades substantially at $t{=}0.9$ ($-$15.7\,pp), which indicates that depth fingerprinting is sensitive to decoding temperature and operates most reliably under standard or conservative sampling regimes.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The near-stationarity of shape features is consistent with the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constraining distributional shape while allowing location to drift.
Temperature ablation supports this as a tendency rather than a guarantee: the signal strengthens at $t{=}0.5$ (+10.4\,pp) but degrades at $t{=}0.9$ ($-$15.7\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and prompt-type dependence further modulates the effect (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).

Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker fingerprints in preliminary experiments (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base, 6-generator LOGO): alignment-imposed length regulation and format constraints compress the distributional variation that DDR exploits.
This restricts current applicability to base models and constitutes the primary scope limitation.
At the document level within base models, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging; the gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ boundary concentrates 86\% of binary errors as false negatives, with larger generators exacerbating this (Mistral-7B error rate 45\% vs.\ Pythia-1B 18\%; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially ($t{=}0.7 \to t{=}1.0$: Qwen3-1.7B F1 drops from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).
A scale-dependent degradation trend is visible: binary F1 decreases from 0.718--0.724 (1--2.8B parameters) to 0.692 (8B) and 0.633 (7B), consistent with larger models compressing the feature margins DDR exploits.

Three classes represent the practical resolution ceiling: 5-class F1 drops to ${\approx}$0.50 (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), and ordinal-specific methods (CORAL, Frank-Hall) yield no improvement over standard XGBoost (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}). These results suggest that the gen-1/gen-2+ boundary rather than ordinal structure is the bottleneck.
DDR is distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: inference-chain drift occurs with fixed parameters, is fully reversible, and leaves distributional shape comparatively stable. This pattern suggests compression within existing capacity rather than erosion of it.
Levene tests reject strict equal-variance for all features ($p < 10^{-10}$), but shape-feature variance ratios (0.98--1.12) are an order of magnitude closer to unity than drifting-feature ratios (1.90--2.20), supporting the characterization as comparatively stable rather than strictly invariant.

\subsection*{Sampling Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{app:sampling-sensitivity}

To assess robustness to decoding temperature, we regenerate continuation chains at $t \in \{0.5, 0.9\}$ with fixed nucleus $p{=}0.9$ (matching the default) for two generators from different families: Pythia-2.8B and Qwen3-1.7B. Evaluation uses within-model 5-fold CV (Table~\ref{tab:sampling-ablation}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Depth classification under varying temperature (fixed top-$p$\,=\,0.9). Binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+. Within-model 5-fold CV; 95\% bootstrap CIs.}
\label{tab:sampling-ablation}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcc cc}
\toprule
Model & Temp & Top-$p$ & Binary F1 & 95\% CI & $\rho$(ent.\ mean) \\
\midrule
Pythia-2.8B & 0.5  & 0.9 & \textbf{0.843} & [.830, .856] & $-0.58$ \\
Pythia-2.8B & 0.7  & 0.9 & 0.739 & --- & $-0.60$ \\
Pythia-2.8B & 0.9  & 0.9 & 0.582 & [.566, .599] & $-0.30$ \\
\midrule
Qwen3-1.7B & 0.7  & 0.9 & --- & --- & $-0.60$ \\
Qwen3-1.7B & 0.9  & 0.9 & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\emph{evaluation pending}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The two generators show qualitatively different sensitivity profiles. Pythia-2.8B improves at lower temperature ($t{=}0.5$: $+$10.4\,pp vs.\ default), consistent with reduced sampling noise preserving more distributional structure, but degrades substantially at $t{=}0.9$ ($-$15.7\,pp).
Entropy mean's Spearman correlation with depth remains strong at $t \leq 0.7$ ($|\rho| \geq 0.58$) but weakens to $|\rho| = 0.30$ at $t{=}0.9$.
This is consistent with the hypothesis that depth features are shaped by the sampling mechanism (\S\ref{sec:discussion}): elevated temperature injects sufficient randomness to flatten the distributional drift that accumulates across generation steps, progressively masking the depth signal.
The practical implication is that depth fingerprinting operates most reliably under standard or conservative decoding regimes ($t \leq 0.7$) and degrades under high-entropy sampling.

we repeat the 6-generator LOGO evaluation using Logistic Regression and Random Forest
in place of XGBoost (Table~\ref{tab:alt-classifier}).
All other settings (the same 7 features, 3-class labels, and class-balanced downsampling) are
kept identical. For Logistic Regression we apply standard scaling to the features.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 across three classifiers. Each column shows the held-out generator F1. (6-generator LOGO; 3-class.)}
\label{tab:alt-classifier}
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lc cccccc}
\toprule
Classifier & Avg F1 & OLMo-2 & Py-1B & Py-2.8B & Qw-0.6B & Qw-1.7B & Qw-8B \\
\midrule
XGBoost          & 0.789 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.824 & 0.806 & 0.683 \\
Random Forest    & 0.790 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.825 & 0.807 & 0.684 \\
Logistic Regr.   & 0.725 & 0.719 & 0.781 & 0.740 & 0.745 & 0.743 & 0.624 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Both tree-based classifiers achieve LOGO F1 $\approx 0.79$,
and even a linear model reaches $0.725$, well above the $0.33$ chance baseline for
three classes.
The per-generator ranking is also consistent across classifiers
(Pythia-1B easiest, Qwen3-8B hardest),
confirming that discriminative power originates in the entropy and lexical features,
not in classifier capacity.
Ordinal-specific methods (CORAL \cite{coral_ordinal}, Frank-Hall \cite{frank_hall_ordinal}) achieve comparable F1 with overlapping CIs, which confirms that 3-class granularity provides insufficient resolution for ranking-aware losses to improve over standard multiclass classification.

\subsection*{Sampling Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{app:sampling-sensitivity}

To assess robustness to decoding temperature, we regenerate Pythia-2.8B continuation chains at $t \in \{0.5, 0.9\}$ with fixed nucleus $p{=}0.9$ (matching the default) and compare against the $t{=}0.7$ baseline. Evaluation uses within-model 5-fold CV on Pythia-2.8B data (Table~\ref{tab:sampling-ablation}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Depth classification under varying temperature (Pythia-2.8B, fixed top-$p$\,=\,0.9). Binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+. Within-model 5-fold CV; 95\% bootstrap CIs.}
\label{tab:sampling-ablation}
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcc cc}
\toprule
Temp & Top-$p$ & Binary F1 & 95\% CI & $\rho$(ent.\ mean) \\
\midrule
0.5  & 0.9 & \textbf{0.843} & [.830, .856] & $-0.58$ \\
0.7  & 0.9 & 0.739 & --- & $-0.60$ \\
0.9  & 0.9 & 0.582 & [.566, .599] & $-0.30$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Depth signal strength varies monotonically with temperature: lowering to $t{=}0.5$ improves binary F1 by 10.4\,pp, while raising to $t{=}0.9$ degrades by 15.7\,pp.
Entropy mean's Spearman correlation with depth remains strong at $t \leq 0.7$ ($|\rho| \geq 0.58$) but weakens to $|\rho| = 0.30$ at $t{=}0.9$.
This is consistent with the hypothesis that depth features are shaped by the sampling mechanism (\S\ref{sec:discussion}): elevated temperature injects sufficient randomness to flatten the distributional drift that accumulates across generation steps, progressively masking the depth signal.
The practical implication is that depth fingerprinting operates most reliably under standard or conservative decoding regimes ($t \leq 0.7$) and degrades under high-entropy sampling.

\subsection*{Per-Generator Performance}

Figure~\ref{fig:per-gen} visualizes per-generator LOGO performance.
Pythia models (1B, 2.8B) achieve highest F1, while larger models (Mistral-7B, Qwen3-8B) show degradation.
The scale effect (larger models $\rightarrow$ lower F1) is consistent with higher-capacity models generating text statistically closer to human writing.

\begin{figure*}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_appendix_per_gen.pdf}
\caption{Per-generator LOGO performance. (a) 8-generator binary and 3-class F1, sorted by binary F1. Dashed lines: pool average. (b) 6-generator LOGO detail heatmap showing the performance spread across model families.}

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects and enable controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base); these comparisons use earlier LOGO subsets (5--6 generators) predating the full 8-generator expansion in Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}.
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730), rewriting (0.737), and paraphrastic chains (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The near-stationarity of shape features is consistent with the softmax architecture and fixed sampling parameters constraining distributional shape while allowing location to drift.
Temperature ablation supports this as a tendency rather than a guarantee: within $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ the signal is preserved (Pythia-2.8B improves at lower temperature, Qwen3-1.7B is stable), but at $t{=}0.9$ it degrades substantially ($-$15.7\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and prompt-type dependence further modulates the effect (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).

Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker fingerprints in preliminary experiments (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.763 base, 6-generator LOGO): alignment-imposed length regulation and format constraints compress the distributional variation that DDR exploits.
This restricts current applicability to base models and constitutes the primary scope limitation.
At the document level within base models, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging; the gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ boundary concentrates 86\% of binary errors as false negatives, with larger generators exacerbating this (Mistral-7B error rate 45\% vs.\ Pythia-1B 18\%; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades substantially ($t{=}0.7 \to t{=}1.0$: Qwen3-1.7B F1 drops from 0.789 to 0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}).
A scale-dependent degradation trend is visible: binary F1 decreases from 0.718--0.724 (1--2.8B parameters) to 0.692 (8B) and 0.633 (7B), consistent with larger models compressing the feature margins DDR exploits.

Three classes represent the practical resolution ceiling: 5-class F1 drops to ${\approx}$0.50 (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}), and ordinal-specific methods (CORAL, Frank-Hall) yield no improvement over standard XGBoost (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}). These results suggest that the gen-1/gen-2+ boundary rather than ordinal structure is the bottleneck.
DDR is distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: inference-chain drift occurs with fixed parameters, is fully reversible, and leaves distributional shape comparatively stable. This pattern suggests compression within existing capacity rather than erosion of it.
Levene tests reject strict equal-variance for all features ($p < 10^{-10}$), but shape-feature variance ratios (0.98--1.12) are an order of magnitude closer to unity than drifting-feature ratios (1.90--2.20), supporting the characterization as comparatively stable rather than strictly invariant.

To verify that the depth signal resides in the features rather than the classifier,
we repeat the 6-generator LOGO evaluation using Logistic Regression and Random Forest
in place of XGBoost (Table~\ref{tab:alt-classifier}).
All other settings (the same 7 features, 3-class labels, and class-balanced downsampling) are
kept identical. For Logistic Regression we apply standard scaling to the features.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 across three classifiers. Each column shows the held-out generator F1. (6-generator LOGO; 3-class.)}
\label{tab:alt-classifier}
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lc cccccc}
\toprule
Classifier & Avg F1 & OLMo-2 & Py-1B & Py-2.8B & Qw-0.6B & Qw-1.7B & Qw-8B \\
\midrule

Logistic Regr.   & 0.725 & 0.719 & 0.781 & 0.740 & 0.745 & 0.743 & 0.624 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Both tree-based classifiers achieve LOGO F1 $\approx 0.79$,
and even a linear model reaches $0.725$, well above the $0.33$ chance baseline for
three classes.
The per-generator ranking is also consistent across classifiers
(Pythia-1B easiest, Qwen3-8B hardest),
confirming that discriminative power originates in the entropy and lexical features,
not in classifier capacity.
Ordinal-specific methods (CORAL \cite{coral_ordinal}, Frank-Hall \cite{frank_hall_ordinal}) achieve comparable F1 with overlapping CIs, which confirms that 3-class granularity provides insufficient resolution for ranking-aware losses to improve over standard multiclass classification.

\midrule
Qwen3-1.7B & 0.7  & 0.9 & --- & --- & $-0.60$ \\

To verify that the depth signal resides in the features rather than the classifier,
we repeat the 6-generator LOGO evaluation using Logistic Regression and Random Forest
in place of XGBoost (Table~\ref{tab:alt-classifier}).
All other settings (the same 7 features, 3-class labels, and class-balanced downsampling) are
kept identical. For Logistic Regression we apply standard scaling to the features.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{LOGO macro-F1 across three classifiers. Each column shows the held-out generator F1. (6-generator LOGO; 3-class.)}
\label{tab:alt-classifier}
\small
\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{lc cccccc}
\toprule
Classifier & Avg F1 & OLMo-2 & Py-1B & Py-2.8B & Qw-0.6B & Qw-1.7B & Qw-8B \\
\midrule
XGBoost          & 0.789 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.824 & 0.806 & 0.683 \\
Random Forest    & 0.790 & 0.764 & 0.856 & 0.804 & 0.825 & 0.807 & 0.684 \\
Logistic Regr.   & 0.725 & 0.719 & 0.781 & 0.740 & 0.745 & 0.743 & 0.624 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

Both tree-based classifiers achieve LOGO F1 $\approx 0.79$,
and even a linear model reaches $0.725$, well above the $0.33$ chance baseline for
three classes.
The per-generator ranking is also consistent across classifiers
(Pythia-1B easiest, Qwen3-8B hardest),
confirming that discriminative power originates in the entropy and lexical features,
not in classifier capacity.
Ordinal-specific methods (CORAL \cite{coral_ordinal}, Frank-Hall \cite{frank_hall_ordinal}) achieve comparable F1 with overlapping CIs, which confirms that 3-class granularity provides insufficient resolution for ranking-aware losses to improve over standard multiclass classification.

\subsection*{Sampling Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{app:sampling-sensitivity}

To assess robustness to decoding temperature, we regenerate continuation chains at $t \in \{0.5, 0.9\}$ with fixed nucleus $p{=}0.9$ (matching the default) for two generators from different families: Pythia-2.8B and Qwen3-1.7B. Evaluation uses the same LOGO protocol as the main experiments (Table~\ref{tab:sampling-ablation}).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Depth classification under varying temperature (fixed top-$p$\,=\,0.9). Binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+. LOGO evaluation; 95\% bootstrap CIs.}
\label{tab:sampling-ablation}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llcc c}
\toprule
Model & Temp & LOGO Binary F1 & 95\% CI & $\rho$(ent.\ mean) \\
\midrule
Pythia-2.8B & 0.5  & \textbf{0.814} & [.798, .828] & $-0.58$ \\
Pythia-2.8B & 0.7  & 0.740 & [.707, .742] & $-0.60$ \\
Pythia-2.8B & 0.9  & 0.480 & [.465, .498] & $-0.30$ \\
\midrule
Qwen3-1.7B & 0.5  & 0.751 & --- & $-0.60$ \\
Qwen3-1.7B & 0.7  & 0.751 & --- & $-0.60$ \\
Qwen3-1.7B & 0.9  & \multicolumn{3}{c}{\emph{evaluation pending}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The two generators show qualitatively different sensitivity profiles. Pythia-2.8B improves at lower temperature ($t{=}0.5$: $+$7.4\,pp vs.\ default), consistent with reduced sampling noise preserving more distributional structure, but degrades sharply at $t{=}0.9$ ($-$26.0\,pp). Qwen3-1.7B shows negligible variation between $t{=}0.5$ and $t{=}0.7$ (0.751 at both).
Entropy mean's Spearman correlation with depth remains strong at $t \leq 0.7$ ($|\rho| \geq 0.58$) but weakens to $|\rho| = 0.30$ at $t{=}0.9$.
This is consistent with the hypothesis that depth features are shaped by the sampling mechanism (\S\ref{sec:discussion}): elevated temperature injects sufficient randomness to flatten the distributional drift that accumulates across generation steps, progressively masking the depth signal.
The practical implication is that depth fingerprinting operates most reliably under standard or conservative decoding regimes ($t \leq 0.7$) and degrades under high-entropy sampling.

\subsection*{Per-Generator Performance}

Figure~\ref{fig:per-gen} visualizes per-generator LOGO performance.
Pythia models (1B, 2.8B) achieve highest F1, while larger models (Mistral-7B, Qwen3-8B) show degradation.
The scale effect (larger models $\rightarrow$ lower F1) is consistent with higher-capacity models generating text statistically closer to human writing.
